implementation_notes: C# async/await is the compiler-generated stackless coroutine: an async method becomes a state machine whose awaiters receive the continuation, and await is the syntax. ValueTask<T> is the allocation-free variant for a result that is usually produced synchronously - it avoids the Task allocation that AsyncTaskMethodBuilder makes - and ValueTask should be used for the await-once-and-don't-cache case. ConfigureAwait(false) is the other decision: it tells the continuation not to capture the synchronization context, which avoids a deadlock when blocking synchronously on a task (the classic ASP.NET classic / UI deadlock) and costs nothing on a server. AsyncLocal flows the execution context across a suspension, which is how a transaction or a security principal follows the logical call chain.
idiom_name: async/await compiler state machine; ValueTask<T> for the allocation-free path; ConfigureAwait(false) to avoid context capture; AsyncLocal for context flow
pitfalls: Calling .Result or .Wait() inside an async method deadlocks under a single-threaded synchronization context - this is the canonical C# async bug.
ConfigureAwait(false) is needed before a blocking wait to avoid the context deadlock; on a server it is also marginally faster.
ValueTask<T> must be awaited exactly once and not stored - it may wrap a pooled IValueTaskSource, and consuming it twice is undefined behaviour.
An async method returning Task allocates the state machine box even on the synchronous path; that is the cost ValueTask avoids.
Thread-local state does not flow across a suspension; use AsyncLocal, or the transaction/principal is lost between awaits.
